title: Aspirin and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Stomach Bleeding Risk and Timing
excerpt: Can you take aspirin after drinking? How aspirin and alcohol affect your stomach and blood clotting, how long to wait, hidden aspirin to watch for, and the warning signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you take aspirin after drinking? How aspirin and alcohol raise stomach bleeding risk, how long to wait, daily low-dose aspirin, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most healthy adults, one standard dose of aspirin the morning after a few drinks is unlikely to cause harm. But aspirin and alcohol share a weak spot, and it is your stomach. Both irritate the stomach lining, and both make it harder for your blood to clot. Put them together and the risk of stomach bleeding goes up, which is why every US over-the-counter aspirin label warns people who have 3 or more drinks a day to ask a doctor first. Aspirin also has a lesser-known twist: some research suggests it can raise your blood alcohol level if you take it before or while drinking. This guide explains both problems, how long to wait, how much is too much, and the warning signs that need medical care.

**The quick rules:** Don't take aspirin before or during a night of drinking to "get ahead" of a hangover. If you do take it the morning after, take one standard dose with food and a full glass of water, and don't stack it with other aspirin-containing products like Alka-Seltzer, Excedrin, or BC and Goody's powders. If you take a daily low-dose aspirin for your heart, don't stop it on your own, but do ask your doctor how much alcohol is safe for you. If you vomit blood, see black or tarry stools, or have severe stomach pain, get emergency care.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining aspirin and alcohol if** you have 3 or more drinks most days, you have had a stomach ulcer or bleeding, you take a blood thinner, steroid, or antidepressant, you take daily aspirin for your heart, you have kidney disease, asthma, or a bleeding disorder, or you are over 60. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, pass black or tarry stools, have severe stomach pain, or feel faint. If you think someone took too much aspirin, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## How Aspirin and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Aspirin is the oldest member of the NSAID family (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), which also includes ibuprofen and naproxen. It relieves pain, lowers fever, and calms inflammation by blocking enzymes called **COX-1 and COX-2**. Those enzymes make prostaglandins, the chemical signals behind pain and swelling.

The trouble is that prostaglandins also do useful jobs. In your stomach, they help produce the mucus layer and bicarbonate that protect the lining from your own stomach acid, and they keep blood flowing to that lining so it can repair itself. When aspirin blocks COX-1, that protection weakens.

Aspirin is also different from the other NSAIDs in one important way. Ibuprofen and naproxen block COX enzymes temporarily, and the effect wears off as the drug leaves your body. Aspirin **permanently** disables the COX-1 enzyme in your platelets, the small blood cells that clump together to stop bleeding. Platelets can't make new enzyme, so a single aspirin dose affects every platelet it touches for the rest of that platelet's life, roughly 7 to 10 days. That's why doctors ask people to stop aspirin a week or more before surgery, and why aspirin is used to prevent heart attacks.

Now add alcohol, which causes trouble along three separate lines.

### 1. Both irritate the stomach lining

Alcohol is a direct irritant to the stomach. Heavy drinking can cause gastritis (inflammation of the stomach lining), and it increases acid production. Aspirin weakens the lining's defenses at the same time. Together they make small erosions and, in some people, bleeding ulcers more likely. Taking aspirin on an empty stomach after a night of drinking is close to the worst setup for this.

### 2. Both make bleeding harder to stop

Aspirin stops platelets from sticking together. Alcohol has its own mild effect on platelet function and clotting. Research going back decades has looked at this pairing; a study published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in 1982 reported that alcohol increased aspirin's effect on bleeding time, a basic lab measure of how quickly a small cut stops bleeding. In practice, this means a stomach erosion that might have stopped on its own is more likely to keep bleeding.

### 3. Aspirin may raise your blood alcohol level

This one surprises people. Some alcohol is broken down in the stomach before it ever reaches your bloodstream, by an enzyme called gastric alcohol dehydrogenase. A small study published in *JAMA* in 1990 found that taking aspirin before drinking reduced this stomach enzyme's activity and led to higher blood alcohol concentrations than drinking alone. Later studies have produced mixed results, and the size of the effect seems to vary from person to person. The practical takeaway is simple: taking aspirin before you drink doesn't protect you from anything, and it may make the same number of drinks hit a little harder.

## What the Labels and Guidance Actually Say

The clearest official guidance comes straight from the Drug Facts label. In the US, over-the-counter aspirin products carry a **stomach bleeding warning**, required by the FDA for oral NSAID pain relievers. It says the chance of stomach bleeding is higher if you:

- are age 60 or older
- have had stomach ulcers or bleeding problems
- take a blood thinner (anticoagulant) or steroid drug
- take other drugs containing prescription or nonprescription NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, or others)
- **have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using this product**
- take more or for a longer time than directed

That "3 or more drinks every day" line is the same threshold that appears on Tylenol, Advil, and Aleve labels. It doesn't mean two drinks are risk-free, and it doesn't mean one aspirin after a big night will cause a bleed. It marks the point at which regulators decided the risk was high enough that people should get a professional's input first.

Beyond the label, clinical research on NSAIDs and alcohol has repeatedly found that the combination raises the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding compared with either one alone, and that the risk grows with more alcohol, higher NSAID doses, longer use, and older age. That pattern matches what the mechanism predicts.

## Can You Take Aspirin After Drinking?

For a healthy adult who drinks occasionally, a single standard dose of aspirin the morning after is generally considered low risk. The risk climbs with a few specific factors:

| Situation | General guidance |
|---|---|
| Healthy adult, occasional drinker | One standard dose (325 to 650 mg for regular strength) with food and water the morning after is generally low risk. Don't exceed the label. |
| Regular drinker (3+ drinks most days) | The label says ask a doctor before use. Stomach bleeding risk is meaningfully higher. |
| History of ulcers or GI bleeding | Avoid unless a doctor says otherwise. Ask about a safer alternative. |
| On a blood thinner, steroid, or SSRI antidepressant | Ask a doctor or pharmacist first. These add to bleeding risk. |
| Daily low-dose aspirin for your heart | Keep taking it as prescribed, but ask your doctor about alcohol. Don't add extra aspirin for a hangover on top. |
| Still drunk or drinking | Wait. Aspirin while alcohol is in your stomach may raise blood alcohol and adds stomach stress. |

A few practical points make a real difference:

- **Eat first.** Food buffers the stomach and slows the contact between aspirin and the lining.
- **Drink a full glass of water.** It helps the tablet move through and you're probably dehydrated anyway.
- **One dose, then reassess.** More aspirin won't fix your headache faster. It only adds stomach and bleeding risk.
- **Enteric-coated aspirin isn't a loophole.** The coating stops the tablet dissolving in the stomach, which may reduce direct irritation, but aspirin's effect on stomach-protecting prostaglandins and on platelets happens through your bloodstream. Coated aspirin can still cause stomach bleeding.

## How Long After Drinking Should You Wait to Take Aspirin?

There's no official waiting time that applies to everyone, and anyone who gives you an exact number of hours is guessing. What we can say with confidence:

- **Wait until the alcohol has cleared.** Your body processes roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot with body size, sex, genetics, food, and how much you drank. After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your system the next morning.
- **Wait until you can keep food down.** If you're still nauseous or vomiting, your stomach is already irritated, and aspirin will make it worse. Rehydrate and eat something bland first.
- **Space it from other painkillers.** If you already took Excedrin or Alka-Seltzer, you've already had aspirin. Don't add more.

In the other direction, if you took aspirin and are wondering how long to wait before drinking, remember that aspirin's effect on platelets lasts for days, even though its pain-relieving effect fades in a few hours. Moderate drinking later that day isn't an emergency for a healthy person, but if you have any of the risk factors in the table above, keep alcohol light or skip it.

## Aspirin for a Hangover: Does It Help?

Aspirin can take the edge off a hangover headache and body aches. That's about all a painkiller can do. Some researchers think inflammation plays a role in hangover symptoms, which is one reason anti-inflammatory drugs like aspirin are sometimes preferred over acetaminophen. But there is no good evidence that aspirin treats a hangover as a whole. It won't help with dehydration, fatigue, poor sleep, low blood sugar, or the general foggy feeling, and it can make an upset stomach worse.

Here's how aspirin compares with the other common options after a night of drinking:

| Painkiller | Main concern with alcohol | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Aspirin | Stomach irritation and bleeding; longer-lasting effect on clotting | May raise blood alcohol if taken before drinking. Not for children or teens. |
| Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) | Stomach irritation and bleeding; kidney strain when dehydrated | Effect on clotting wears off as the drug clears. See our [ibuprofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol). |
| Naproxen (Aleve) | Same stomach and kidney concerns, longer-lasting dose | One dose lasts 8 to 12 hours. See our [Aleve and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol). |
| Acetaminophen (Tylenol) | Liver injury, especially with regular heavy drinking or high doses | Easier on the stomach, harder on the liver. See our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). |

None of these is risk-free after heavy drinking. The "best" choice depends on your own body: people with stomach problems often do better avoiding NSAIDs, and people who drink heavily on a regular basis need to be careful with acetaminophen. A pharmacist can help you pick, and it takes about five minutes.

### Don't take aspirin "pre-emptively"

A popular piece of folk advice is to take a couple of aspirin before bed after drinking so you wake up without a headache. This is a bad idea for three reasons. Alcohol is still in your stomach and bloodstream, so you get the full stomach-irritation overlap. You're probably taking it without food. And if you take it before or during drinking, it may raise your blood alcohol. If you wake up with a headache, deal with it then, after you've eaten. For headache-specific tactics that don't rely on pills, see our guide to [hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

## Hidden Aspirin: Check Before You Double Up

Aspirin is in more products than people realize, and several are marketed directly at the morning after. Taking two of these together can push you well past a sensible dose without noticing.

Common places aspirin shows up:

- **Alka-Seltzer Original**, an effervescent tablet that combines aspirin with sodium bicarbonate and citric acid. It's often sold as a hangover remedy. The bicarbonate is also a lot of sodium, which matters if you have high blood pressure.
- **Excedrin** (Extra Strength and Migraine), which pairs aspirin with acetaminophen and caffeine. That means you get the stomach risk of aspirin and the liver concern of Tylenol at the same time. Our [Excedrin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/excedrin-and-alcohol) covers this in detail.
- **BC Powder and Goody's Powder**, which deliver a large dose of aspirin quickly, often with caffeine.
- **Hangover-branded products** such as [Blowfish](/never-hungover/blowfish-hangover-review), which contains aspirin with caffeine.
- **Some prescription combination pills** that include aspirin.

A related one to know about is **Pepto-Bismol**. Its active ingredient, bismuth subsalicylate, is chemically related to aspirin. Its label warns people who are allergic to aspirin or who take blood thinners, and combining it with aspirin adds to your total salicylate load. If you reach for Pepto for a queasy stomach and aspirin for a headache on the same morning, ask a pharmacist first.

On labels, look for **aspirin**, **acetylsalicylic acid**, or **salicylate** in the Drug Facts box.

## How Much Aspirin Is Too Much?

Follow the label on your specific product, because strengths and directions vary. As a general guide for adults:

- **Regular strength** is 325 mg per tablet. **Extra strength** is usually 500 mg. **Low-dose** ("baby") aspirin is 81 mg.
- OTC labels for regular-strength aspirin typically allow 1 to 2 tablets every 4 hours, with a daily ceiling of about 4,000 mg (12 tablets of 325 mg) in 24 hours. Many people need far less, and with alcohol in the picture, staying at the low end is wiser.
- The label tells you to stop and ask a doctor if pain lasts more than 10 days or fever more than 3 days.

Taking too much aspirin causes **salicylate poisoning**, which is a real emergency. Early signs include **ringing in the ears**, nausea, vomiting, fast or deep breathing, and sweating. Later signs include confusion, agitation, drowsiness, and fever. Some of these overlap with a bad hangover, which is exactly why it's worth keeping count. If you think someone has taken too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) right away, even if they seem okay.

**Never give aspirin to children or teenagers** for a fever or viral illness. Aspirin in young people recovering from flu or chickenpox is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious condition affecting the liver and brain.

## Daily Low-Dose Aspirin and Alcohol

Many people take 81 mg of aspirin every day because a doctor prescribed it after a heart attack, stroke, or stent, or because of other cardiovascular risk. If that's you, two things are true at the same time.

First, **don't stop prescribed aspirin on your own**, including on days you plan to drink. For people who already have heart disease, stopping aspirin suddenly can raise the risk of a heart attack or stroke.

Second, alcohol does add to the bleeding risk of daily aspirin, even at a low dose. Long-term daily aspirin already carries a known risk of stomach bleeding, and regular drinking raises it. That doesn't mean you can never have a glass of wine. It means the right amount of alcohol for you is a conversation to have with your doctor, who may also suggest stomach protection, such as an acid-reducing medicine, if your bleeding risk is high.

If you take daily aspirin for **prevention only** and nobody has reviewed that decision in a while, it's worth asking about. US guidance on routine aspirin for people without heart disease has become more cautious in recent years, because for many people the bleeding risk can outweigh the benefit. That's a decision for you and your doctor, not something to change based on an article.

And one practical rule: if you're already on daily aspirin, don't add regular-strength aspirin on top for a hangover headache without asking a pharmacist. You'd be stacking two doses of the same drug.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Stomach bleeding can be sudden and obvious, or slow and easy to miss. Know both pictures.

**Go to the emergency room or call 911 if you notice:**

- Vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like **coffee grounds**
- **Black, tarry, or bloody stools**
- Severe or persistent stomach pain
- Feeling faint, dizzy when standing, a racing heart, or unusual paleness, which can signal blood loss

**Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if:**

- You may have taken more aspirin than the label allows, or took several aspirin-containing products
- You develop ringing in the ears, rapid breathing, or confusion after taking aspirin

**See a doctor soon if:**

- You get ongoing stomach pain, heartburn, or indigestion when you take aspirin
- You bruise easily or have unusual bleeding from your gums or nose
- You need a painkiller after drinking most mornings, which is itself worth talking about

People with asthma should also know that some of them are sensitive to aspirin and other NSAIDs, and in those people alcohol can also trigger breathing symptoms. If aspirin has ever made your breathing worse, avoid it and ask your doctor about alternatives.

## Who Should Avoid Aspirin With Alcohol

Be most careful, and ask a doctor or pharmacist first, if you:

- Have **3 or more drinks most days**, or binge drink regularly
- Have had a **stomach ulcer, gastritis, or GI bleeding**
- Take a **blood thinner** such as warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, or clopidogrel
- Take a **steroid** such as prednisone
- Take an **SSRI or SNRI antidepressant**, which can also increase bleeding risk
- Take another **NSAID** regularly, including ibuprofen or naproxen
- Are **60 or older**
- Have **kidney disease**, **liver disease**, a **bleeding disorder**, or **aspirin-sensitive asthma**
- Are **pregnant**, especially later in pregnancy, unless your doctor has prescribed it
- Have **gout**, since aspirin can affect uric acid levels and alcohol is a common gout trigger

Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers how common medicines interact with supplements and alcohol more broadly.

## A Better Path: Prevent the Headache Instead of Treating It

Aspirin treats a symptom, and after drinking it does so at the cost of some stomach risk. If you're reading about aspirin and alcohol because you regularly wake up reaching for painkillers, the most effective changes are the plain ones: drink less, pace yourself, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, eat a real meal beforehand, and protect your sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence behind them.

Some people also try supplements. Here's an honest view of where the most popular one stands.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than settled. It is not a painkiller, it does not protect your stomach from aspirin, and there is no good evidence that it reduces the bleeding risk of combining aspirin and alcohol. If you want to try DHM as part of a sensible drinking routine, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take daily aspirin or any blood thinner, check with your doctor before adding any supplement.

Whatever you take, no supplement changes the aspirin rules: follow the label, take it with food, don't double up on hidden aspirin, and respect the alcohol warning.

## The Bottom Line

- One standard dose of aspirin with food the morning after a few drinks is generally low risk for a healthy adult who drinks occasionally.
- Aspirin and alcohol both irritate the stomach and both interfere with clotting, so together they raise the risk of stomach bleeding. The label says to ask a doctor first if you have 3 or more drinks every day.
- Don't take aspirin before or during drinking. It doesn't prevent a hangover and may raise your blood alcohol level.
- Watch for hidden aspirin in Alka-Seltzer, Excedrin, BC and Goody's powders, and hangover-branded products.
- If you take daily aspirin for your heart, keep taking it and ask your doctor how much alcohol is safe for you.
- Vomiting blood, coffee-ground vomit, or black stools is an emergency. Call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I take aspirin after drinking alcohol?**

For most healthy adults who drink occasionally, one standard dose of aspirin with food and water the morning after a few drinks is generally low risk. Wait until the alcohol has cleared and you can keep food down. If you have 3 or more drinks most days, have had a stomach ulcer or bleeding, take a blood thinner, steroid, or antidepressant, or are over 60, ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking aspirin after drinking.

**How long after drinking can I take aspirin?**

There is no official waiting period that applies to everyone. A sensible approach is to wait until the alcohol is out of your system (the body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies), eat something first, and then take a single standard dose with a full glass of water. If you are still nauseous or vomiting, wait longer, because aspirin will irritate an already upset stomach.

**Is aspirin good for a hangover?**

Aspirin can ease a hangover headache and body aches, but there is no good evidence that it treats a hangover as a whole. It does nothing for dehydration, fatigue, or poor sleep, and it can make an upset stomach worse after drinking. If you use it, take one dose with food rather than on an empty stomach.

**Should I take aspirin before drinking to prevent a hangover?**

No. Taking aspirin before or while drinking doesn't prevent a hangover, adds stress to a stomach that alcohol is already irritating, and may raise your blood alcohol level. A small 1990 study in JAMA found higher blood alcohol levels when aspirin was taken before drinking, although later studies have been mixed. If you wake up with a headache, deal with it then, after eating.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking daily low-dose aspirin?**

Many people on daily low-dose aspirin can drink moderately, but alcohol does add to aspirin's bleeding risk, so ask your doctor what amount is safe for you. Do not stop prescribed aspirin on your own, especially if you have heart disease or a stent, and don't add extra aspirin for a hangover on top of your daily dose without asking a pharmacist.

**What are the signs of stomach bleeding from aspirin and alcohol?**

Warning signs include vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or tarry stools, severe or ongoing stomach pain, and feeling faint, dizzy, or unusually pale. These need emergency care, so call 911 or go to the emergency room. Milder ongoing stomach pain or heartburn when you take aspirin is worth seeing a doctor about soon.

**Is aspirin or ibuprofen safer after drinking?**

Both are NSAIDs and carry the same label warning about stomach bleeding for people who have 3 or more drinks a day. Aspirin's effect on blood clotting lasts for days, while ibuprofen's wears off as the drug clears, and aspirin may also raise blood alcohol if taken before drinking. Tylenol is easier on the stomach but harder on the liver. None is risk-free after heavy drinking, so take any of them with food, at the lowest effective dose, and ask a pharmacist if you have risk factors.

**Does DHM protect your stomach from aspirin and alcohol?**

There's no good evidence that DHM protects against stomach irritation or bleeding from aspirin and alcohol. DHM has promising research on alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly from animal studies with limited human data. Follow the aspirin label and alcohol warning regardless of any supplement you take, and check with your doctor before adding supplements if you take daily aspirin or a blood thinner.
